## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
```

## Question 1: New Jersey's individual market, 2000 to 2008

### (a) Build the dataset

The dataset comes from the New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance
Individual Health Coverage (IHC) data. For each year from 2000 to 2008, it has
the monthly family premium for Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield Plan D (\$1,000
deductible), Aetna Plan D (\$1,000 deductible), and Celtic Plan C (\$2,500
deductible), along with total year-end standard enrollment in the IHC program.
The file is `nj-ihc.csv` at the top of this repository, outside the gitignored
`data/` folder so that it is included in the submission.

```{r}
nj <- read_csv("../nj-ihc.csv")

kable(nj, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      col.names = c("Year", "BCBS Plan D", "Aetna Plan D", "Celtic Plan C",
                    "Enrollment"),
      caption = "Monthly family premiums ($) and year-end standard enrollment, NJ IHC")
```

### (b) Make the figure

Premiums and enrollment are in different units, so the figure shows them in two
panels over the same years.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
nj_long <- bind_rows(
  nj %>%
    pivot_longer(c(bcbs_plan_d, aetna_plan_d, celtic_plan_c),
                 names_to = "series", values_to = "value") %>%
    mutate(panel = "Monthly family premium ($)",
           series = recode(series, bcbs_plan_d = "BCBS Plan D",
                           aetna_plan_d = "Aetna Plan D",
                           celtic_plan_c = "Celtic Plan C")),
  nj %>%
    transmute(year, series = "Enrollment", value = enrollment,
              panel = "Year-end standard enrollment")
)

ggplot(nj_long, aes(year, value, group = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(data = nj_long %>% filter(year == 2008, series != "Enrollment"),
            aes(label = series), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2000:2008, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.18))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL,
       title = "NJ individual market: premiums rise as enrollment falls") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#| include: false
first <- nj %>% filter(year == 2000)
last <- nj %>% filter(year == 2008)
```

All three premiums rise sharply over the period. The BCBS Plan D premium goes
from \$`r comma(first$bcbs_plan_d)` a month in 2000 to
\$`r comma(last$bcbs_plan_d)` in 2008, about
`r round(last$bcbs_plan_d / first$bcbs_plan_d, 1)` times as high. Aetna rises
from \$`r comma(first$aetna_plan_d)` to \$`r comma(last$aetna_plan_d)`, and
Celtic from \$`r comma(first$celtic_plan_c)` to \$`r comma(last$celtic_plan_c)`,
with Celtic's premium unchanged from 2003 on. Over the same years, year-end
enrollment falls every year, from `r comma(first$enrollment)` to
`r comma(last$enrollment)`, a decline of about
`r percent(1 - last$enrollment / first$enrollment)`.

### (c) Interpret it

Rising premiums together with falling enrollment is what adverse selection
predicts. The IHC program was guaranteed issue and community rated, so insurers
had to accept every applicant and charge everyone in a plan the same premium.
When premiums rise, the people most likely to drop coverage are the healthiest,
who expect to use the least care and so get the least value from insurance. Their
exit leaves a sicker and more expensive pool, which raises the insurer's average
cost and leads to another premium increase the next year, and the cycle repeats.

### (d) Verdict

Other forces could produce part of this pattern. Health care costs rose across
the whole economy in the 2000s, so some of the premium growth would have happened
without any change in who was enrolled. The IHC market is also small, so a change
by a single insurer, such as a new plan design or a decision to stop marketing a
plan, can move premiums and enrollment on its own.

Even so, the size of the changes points to selection. The BCBS Plan D premium
rose about fourfold in eight years. By comparison, the average employer premium
for family coverage rose 119% from 1999 to 2008, a little more than doubling
([KFF Employer Health Benefits 2008 Annual Survey](https://www.kff.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/04/7790.pdf)). Meanwhile,
enrollment fell by nearly half and kept falling every year. That combination is
hard to explain without healthier people leaving the pool. I read it as a death
spiral in progress, a market unraveling steadily rather than collapsing at once,
since about `r comma(last$enrollment)` people were still enrolled in 2008.
